newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Footprints of locals seen in Manila peso massacre.
newsitem.headline: Footprints of locals seen in Manila peso massacre.

text.p: A probe by the Philippine central bank to find out if speculators had forced a de facto peso devaluation has shown not just foreigners but local investors may have been involved, President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday.
"(There are indications) that it is not all foreign," Ramos told his weekly news conference when asked if the probe had yielded anything so far.
"We have left this (the probe) to the Bangko Sentral (central bank) since it is the government agency that supervises the operations of banks whether foreign, local or otherwise," he said.
Ramos said he felt the investigation to find out if there was a concerted campaign to weaken the peso was essential because common people would suffer from its consequences.

"The probe I felt is timely and necessary because we who are the lay people, the consumers and non-bankers are probably also the widest or the broadest sector in terms of being victimised by all of this."

He added: "We have rendered this last assessment of the Bangko Sentral citing the Hong Kong bank Manila branch as being the conduit for about 80 pct of the investment or dollar flows through our markets, so may be that is one indication that it is not all foreign."

Government officials have earlier said foreign speculators were to blame for the pressure on the peso, which ultimately forced the central bank to announce last Friday that the currency would be allowed to trade in a wider range.
Ramos himself a week ago put the blame squarely on "outsiders" for the speculative attacks on the peso.

The central bank move, which meant an effective devaluation, has sent the peso plunging. On Tuesday, it was at 29.50 pesos to the dollar, down nearly 12 percent from the average 26.50 pesos before the central bank's announcement.
Singson, in a report to the president, said Hong Kong bank had told officials that traders viewed 29-29.50 pesos as a stable level for the currency.
"They had very encouraging information to share," Singson said in the report.
